hints: Look at the black bars in Fig. 2.1 from Na to Cl and recall how many protons are added as you move across Period 3, and whether a new shell is started.
Think about how shielding by inner shells changes across a period and what this means for the pull felt by the outer electrons.
walkthrough:
See what the black bars tell you**
Picture the atoms from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Cl}$. They all have their outer electrons in the n = 3 shell, no new shell is added. At the same time the proton number rises from 11 to 17, so each successive nucleus has more positive charge.

Decide what happens to the pull**
Shielding comes mainly from the full inner shells ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$), which stays almost the same across the period. With more protons pulling and almost the same shielding blocking, the effective pull on the outer shell gets stronger and stronger, so the electron cloud is drawn in closer and the atomic radius falls.

Final answer: Atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl.
Nuclear charge (proton number) increases across the period with similar shielding, so outer electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus.

hints: Write the electron configurations of $\text{Al}$ and $\text{P}$ and work out whether each forms a positive ion by losing electrons or a negative ion by gaining electrons.
Compare the number of occupied shells left in $\text{Al}^{3+}$ with the number in $\text{P}^{3-}$.
walkthrough:
Work out the two opposite ion types**
$\text{Al}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^1$. It is easiest to lose its three outer electrons to get a stable octet, forming $\text{Al}^{3+}$ with configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$. $\text{P}$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$. It is easiest to gain three electrons to fill the 3p subshell, forming $\text{P}^{3-}$ with configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$.

Count the shells that remain**
$\text{Al}^{3+}$ has lost its whole n = 3 shell, so its outermost shell is n = 2. $\text{P}^{3-}$ still uses n = 3 and now has extra electron repulsion in that shell. Losing a whole shell makes the cation very small, while keeping three shells plus added repulsion makes the anion very large, which is why the white bars jump from about 50 pm to over 200 pm.

Final answer: $\text{Al}$ loses 3 electrons to form $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{P}$ gains 3 electrons to form $\text{P}^{3-}$.
$\text{Al}^{3+}$ has one fewer occupied shell than $\text{P}^{3-}$, so it is much smaller.

hints: Use oxygen as -2 in each oxide to calculate the oxidation number of the Period 3 element, for example $2x + (-2) = 0$ for $\text{MgO}$ and $2x + 3(-2) = 0$ for $\text{SO}_3$.
Recall that $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{MgO}$ give alkaline solutions, while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ and $\text{SO}_3$ give strongly acidic solutions.
walkthrough:
Fill in the oxidation numbers**
Take $\text{O}$ as -2. For $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$: $2x -2 = 0$ so $x = +1$. For $\text{MgO}$: $x -2 = 0$ so $x = +2$. For $\text{SiO}_2$: $x -4 = 0$ so $x = +4$. For $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$: $4x -20 = 0$ so $x = +5$. For $\text{SO}_3$: $x -6 = 0$ so $x = +6$. This shows oxidation number rises steadily across the period.

Fill in the pH values**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ forms $\text{NaOH}$, a strong alkali, so pH 12-14. $\text{MgO}$ forms sparingly soluble $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, weakly alkaline, so pH about 8-10. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ forms phosphoric acid and $\text{SO}_3$ forms sulfuric acid, both strong acids, so pH 0-4. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ stay as dashes because they do not give a solution.

Final answer: Row A (oxidation number): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ +1, $\text{MgO}$ +2, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ +3, $\text{SiO}_2$ +4, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ +5, $\text{SO}_3$ +6.
Row B (pH): $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ 12-14, $\text{MgO}$ 8-10, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ -, $\text{SiO}_2$ -, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ 0-4, $\text{SO}_3$ 0-4.

hints: Think about what must happen for a pH value to be measured and why $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ cannot do this in water.
walkthrough:
Link pH to dissolving**
A pH meter only works in an aqueous solution with free $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ ions. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ has a very high lattice energy and $\text{SiO}_2$ is a giant covalent lattice, so neither dissolves or reacts with water to release ions. With no solution formed, row B must be left blank.
Final answer: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ are insoluble in water, so no solution forms and no pH can be measured.

hints: Treat $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ as a strong base that neutralises $\text{HCl}$ to give a sodium salt and water only.
walkthrough:
Build the neutralisation equation**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a basic oxide, so with acid it gives salt plus water. Two $\text{H}^+$ ions are needed to combine with the $\text{O}^{2-}$ to make $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving $2\text{Na}^+$ and $2\text{Cl}^-$ to make $2\text{NaCl}$. Balancing gives $$\text{Na}_2\text{O} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Remember $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric so it reacts with a base like $\text{NaOH}$ to form sodium aluminate, $\text{NaAlO}_2$, plus water.
walkthrough:
Use the amphoteric behaviour**
With acids $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ acts as a base, but with a strong base it acts as an acid and forms the aluminate ion $\text{AlO}_2^-$. Two $\text{NaOH}$ provide the two $\text{Na}^+$ needed for two $\text{NaAlO}_2$ units, and the extra H and O make water: $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Recall how cation size changes down Group 2 and how easily a larger, less polarising cation is distorted by heat.
walkthrough:
Follow stability down the group**
Going down Group 2 the cation gets larger, so its charge density and polarising power fall. It distorts the nitrate ion less, so more heat is needed to break it down. That means magnesium nitrate decomposes most easily and barium nitrate is the most stable to heat.
Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2.

hints: Write the general decomposition $\text{M(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow \text{MO} +$ two gases, and recall the brown gas seen in this test.
walkthrough:
Name the two gases**
All Group 2 nitrates follow $$2\text{M(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ The oxide stays as a solid, while brown nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$, and oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, are evolved as gases.
